value.overview: The White Hawk (Pseudastur albicollis) is a striking forest hawk of tropical Central and South America. Its mostly white plumage, broad dark wing tips, and dark facial markings make it distinctive in flight. It usually hunts from elevated perches, watching for prey below, and is often associated with humid forest and forest edges. In Costa Rica, it is a regularly encountered resident, especially in lowland and foothill regions with suitable forest habitat.
value.classification: The White Hawk belongs to the hawk and eagle family Accipitridae. It is the only species in the genus Pseudastur.
value.identification: Adults are largely white, with black or very dark markings on the outer wings and tail and a dark mask around the eyes. The wings are broad, and the bird often soars with slow, deliberate wingbeats. From below, the contrast between the white body and dark wing tips is especially noticeable. Juveniles are generally browner and less sharply patterned than adults. Its medium-large size and distinctive black-and-white appearance help separate it from other Costa Rican raptors.
value.rangeHabitat: The White Hawk occurs from southern Mexico through Central America and across much of northern and central South America. In Costa Rica, it is found mainly in humid Caribbean-slope forests, foothills, and adjacent forest edges, and it also occurs locally on the Pacific slope where suitable woodland remains. It generally uses lowland and lower montane evergreen forest, river corridors, plantations near forest, and clearings with tall perches. It can occur from sea level into the foothills, but is less typical in heavily cleared areas.
value.migrationStatus: The White Hawk is generally resident in Costa Rica and is not considered a regular long-distance migrant. Individuals may move locally in response to food availability, breeding activity, or habitat conditions.
value.breeding: White Hawks usually breed in mature forest, placing a large stick nest high in a tree, often near the canopy. The nest is built from branches and may be reused or repaired in successive years. The species generally lays a small clutch, commonly a single egg, and both adults participate in territorial defense and care of the young. Breeding timing varies across its broad range; in Costa Rica, nesting may occur during different parts of the year depending on region and local rainfall patterns.
value.dietFeeding: Its diet includes reptiles, amphibians, birds, insects, and other small animals. The White Hawk commonly hunts from a high, exposed perch, scanning the ground and vegetation before making a short flight to capture prey. It may also search along forest edges and clearings. In some areas, it follows groups of foraging monkeys or mixed-species bird flocks, taking advantage of animals disturbed by their movement.
value.behavior: White Hawks are usually seen alone, in pairs, or occasionally in family groups. They spend long periods perched quietly before soaring above the forest or moving between elevated perches. Pairs defend territories and may circle together while calling. Their broad wings and contrasting plumage make them conspicuous when soaring over forest canopies. They are generally less tolerant of extensive open farmland than more adaptable roadside raptors.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not considered to be facing an immediate extinction risk, although local populations may decline where mature forest is lost or fragmented.
